newsitem.title: CHINA: China says cannot open up telecommunications market.
newsitem.headline: China says cannot open up telecommunications market.

text.p: China said on Saturday it would not open its telecommunications fully to foreign companies in the foreseeable future as its market was too immature. The statement, carried by the official Xinhua news agency, quoted Minister of Posts and Telecommunications Wu Jichuan and was said to have been made to Sir Leon Brittan, Vice President of the European Commission.
Brittan was in China earlier this month leading a delegation of European telecoms companies and trying to accelerate China's entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
Barriers to foreign companies entering the domestic telecommunications market are among the many stumbling blocks in the path of China's drive to join the WTO.
China does not permit foreign companies to operate telecommunications networks in its domestic market.
It has allowed foreign firms to sell equipment to China but it has made progressively higher demands for local manufacturing and the transfer of technology.
China's telecommunications market has been expanding at a breakneck pace.
Industry specialists estimate China will add 10 million telephone lines in 1996, bringing the total to more than 60 million by the end of the year.
It is also installing increasingly advanced equipment to modernise its telecommunications services.
Wu was quoted as saying that conditions for a fully open market were not yet mature because China's telecommunications growth relied on preferential government policies.
Unbalanced development in favour of the eastern coastal areas was another problem blocking greater participation by foreign companies, he said without elaborating.
Wu also said that the lack of separation between the telecommunications and postal services was a barrier as the two sectors now subsidise each other, according to Xinhua.
Industry officials say, however, that telecommunications services are highly profitable overall while the postal service requires government subsidies.
